present.explain: A Russian verb's ending says who does it: я пью (I drink), ты пьёшь (you drink), он пьёт (he drinks); я чита́ю, ты чита́ешь, она́ чита́ет; я иду́, ты идёшь, мы идём, вы идёте. Learn each verb's forms as you meet them: пить and идти́ change more than their ending.
present.why: English changes its verb only for he and she; Russian changes it for everyone, so [[пью]] already says I drink. The same form says I drink and I'm drinking: Russian has no -ing.

examples.text: Мы идём домой, а он читает.
examples.means: We're going home, and he's reading.
examples.literal: We go home, and he reads.

contrasts.says: English adds -s only for he and she, and says I'm drinking with -ing; Russian has one form for both, with an ending for each person.
After хочу́ or могу́, the next verb takes no ending: Я хочу́ пить.

mistakes.why: With я, it's пью.
With ты, it's чита́ешь.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

gender.explain: Every Russian noun is a он word, a она́ word or an оно́ word, and the words with it match: оди́н чай, одна́ маши́на; мой телефо́н, моя́ маши́на. Most nouns ending in a consonant are он words (телефо́н, ключ, дом), most ending in -а are она́ words (су́мка, маши́на, ма́ма), and most ending in -о are оно́ words (молоко́). ко́фе is a он word though it ends in -е.
gender.why: English has he, she and it for people and for what you point back to; Russian sorts every noun this way, so a phone is он: Где телефо́н? [[Он]] здесь. Learn which with the word; the ending usually tells you.

examples.means: My coffee is on the table.

contrasts.says: English calls a thing it; Russian calls a телефо́н он and a су́мка она́, as it would a man and a woman.
мой and твой follow the noun's gender: мой ключ, моя́ су́мка.

mistakes.why: телефо́н is a он word: мой.
чай is a он word: оди́н.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

no-be.explain: In the present, Russian says no am, is or are: Я до́ма (I'm at home), Телефо́н на столе́ (the phone is on the table), Где ключ? (where's the key?). The words just stand side by side.
no-be.why: English needs a verb in every sentence; Russian leaves to be out in the present, as an English headline does (Phone on table).

contrasts.says: English can't leave is out (The phone on the table isn't a sentence); Russian always does in the present.
Э́то alone says this is: Э́то мой ключ (this my key).

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

question.explain: A yes/no question keeps a statement's order; only the voice rises on the word asked about (the ? when written): Маши́на здесь. (the car's here) → Маши́на здесь? (is the car here?). A question word (где, что, чей) most often comes first: Где маши́на? Что ты чита́ешь?
question.why: English turns words around or adds do (Do you drink coffee?); Russian changes nothing but the voice: Ты пьёшь ко́фе? There's no do in Russian at all.

contrasts.says: English moves is or adds do (Is the car here? Do you read?); Russian keeps the order and lets the voice ask.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

accusative.explain: What you drink, read or hold takes the accusative. For она́ words ending in -а, the -а becomes -у: вода́ → Я пью во́ду, кни́га → Я чита́ю кни́гу, газе́та → Он чита́ет газе́ту. он and оно́ words stay as they are: Я пью чай, Я пью молоко́.
accusative.why: English shows who does what by order alone; Russian also marks it on the word, so [[во́ду]] is water as what's drunk, wherever it stands.

contrasts.says: English never changes water for what you drink; Russian does: вода́, во́ду.
Where something is takes -е instead: в маши́не, на столе́.

mistakes.why: What you drink: во́ду.
What he reads: кни́гу.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

prepositional.explain: After в (in) and на (on, at), where something is takes the prepositional, mostly ending in -е: стол → на столе́, су́мка → в су́мке, маши́на → в маши́не, рабо́та → на рабо́те.
prepositional.why: English says where with in and on alone; Russian says it twice, with the little word and with the ending, so [[столе́]] after на is the table as a place.

examples.means: The key is on the table.
The phone is in the bag.

contrasts.says: English's on and in change nothing after them; Russian's change the word.
до́ма (at home) and домо́й (home, going there) say it without в or на.

mistakes.why: After в, where it is: су́мке.
After на, where she is: рабо́те.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

possessive.explain: мой (my) and твой (your) match their noun as an adjective does: мой телефо́н, моя́ су́мка; твой ключ, твоя́ маши́на. твой is for someone you say ты to.
possessive.why: English's my never changes; Russian's follows the noun's gender, so [[моя́]] tells you су́мка is a она́ word.

examples.means: Your bag is on the table.

contrasts.says: The noun's gender decides: мой for он words, моя́ for она́ words.
English has one my; Russian has мой and моя́, and more forms you'll meet.

mistakes.why: ключ is a он word: мой.
су́мка is a она́ word: твоя́.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

short-adjective.explain: A few adjectives have a short form for how someone is, and it says the gender: гото́в (a man), гото́ва (a woman), гото́вы (more than one, or вы). Я гото́в. Она́ гото́ва. Мы гото́вы.
short-adjective.why: English's ready is the same for everyone; Russian's says who it's about, so a woman says Я [[гото́ва]] and a man Я гото́в.

contrasts.says: English says ready for anyone; Russian's form says a man, a woman or more than one.
With вы, even to one person, it's гото́вы.

mistakes.why: With мы: гото́вы.
With она́: гото́ва.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

direction.explain: Being somewhere and going there are different words: до́ма is at home, домо́й is home as where you go: Я до́ма (I'm at home), Я иду́ домо́й (I'm going home).
direction.why: English uses home for both; Russian asks where at or where to. A verb of going takes [[домо́й]]; being, drinking or reading there takes до́ма.

contrasts.says: English's home is both; Russian's до́ма is where you are and домо́й where you go.
идти́ (to go) takes домо́й: Я иду́ домо́й.

mistakes.why: Where you are: до́ма.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

ne.explain: не goes right before the word it denies, most often the verb: Я не пью ко́фе (I don't drink coffee), Я не могу́ помо́чь (I can't help). Russian has no do: не alone says don't.
ne.why: English needs do to say not (I don't drink); Russian puts [[не]] in front of the verb and changes nothing else.

contrasts.says: English adds do or does (I don't, she doesn't); Russian never does.
With nothing to have, нет takes есть's place: У меня́ нет рабо́ты.

mistakes.why: Before a verb it's не; нет is no.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

infinitive.explain: After хочу́ (I want), могу́ (I can) and дава́й (let's), the next verb stays in its dictionary form: Я хочу́ пить, Я могу́ помо́чь, Дава́й пить чай.
infinitive.why: English says to after want (I want to drink) and nothing after can; Russian needs neither: the dictionary form, like [[пить]], does it.

contrasts.says: Only the first verb takes the ending: Я хочу́ пить.
English adds to after want; Russian adds nothing.

mistakes.why: After хочу́, the dictionary form: пить.
After могу́: помо́чь.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

have.explain: To say you have something, Russian says it's at you: У меня́ есть рабо́та (at me is work: I have work), У тебя́ есть маши́на? (do you have a car?). With none, нет takes есть's place, and the thing takes the genitive: У меня́ нет рабо́ты.
have.why: English's have is a verb of its own; Russian builds it from у (at) and меня́ (me), so У меня́ есть is I have, and the thing you have is the sentence's subject.

examples.means: I still have work to do.

contrasts.says: English's have is a verb; Russian says the thing is at you.
With нет, the thing takes the genitive: рабо́та becomes рабо́ты.

mistakes.why: What you have stays as it is: рабо́та.
After у, я becomes меня́.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

demonstrative.explain: э́тот (this) matches its noun: э́тот телефо́н, э́та су́мка. э́то on its own says this is or that's, with no is, and never changes: Э́то мой ключ, Э́то су́мка ма́мы.
demonstrative.why: English says this for both; Russian's э́тот points at a thing and matches it, and э́то presents one: Э́то [[маши́на]] ма́мы (this is Mom's car).

contrasts.says: After its noun, мой or моя́ alone says mine: Э́тот телефо́н мой.
Э́то alone says this is.

mistakes.why: су́мка is a она́ word: э́та.
телефо́н is a он word: э́тот.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

address.explain: ты is for one person you know well; вы is for someone you don't know well, or for more than one, and takes the plural verb form: Ты идёшь домо́й? to a friend, Вы идёте домо́й? to a stranger or to two friends.
address.why: English has one you; Russian chooses, and the verb's ending follows: вы [[идёте]].

contrasts.says: English's you is one word for everyone; Russian's says how well you know them, or that there's more than one.
With вы, even to one person, it's гото́вы.

mistakes.why: With вы: идёте.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

question-word.explain: Кто asks who, что what, где where, куда́ where to, отку́да where from, когда́ when and почему́ why. Usually start with the question word. Either the subject or the verb can follow: Куда́ ты идёшь? Куда́ идёт твой друг? Both orders are normal. If кто itself is the subject, the verb is singular: Кто стучи́т? A question about a place needs no is: Где ключ?
question-word.why: English often adds do or moves an auxiliary before the subject. Russian adds no do: Что ты и́щешь? The question word says what information is missing. Where has three useful counterparts: где for a location, куда́ for a destination, отку́да for a starting point.

contrasts.says: English often changes the order and adds do. Russian uses its ordinary verb form: Что ты чита́ешь?
Где asks about a location, as in Где твой дом? Куда́ asks about a destination, as in Куда́ ты идёшь? Отку́да asks about a starting point.
Ты стучи́шь? asks for yes or no. Кто стучи́т? asks for the person. Question words can also come later for emphasis or a follow-up: Ты куда́?

mistakes.why: When кто is the subject, use the third-person singular стучи́т, even when asking the listener who is knocking.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

pronoun-object.explain: When a pronoun names the person heard or seen, it takes its accusative form: я → меня́, ты → тебя́, он → его́, она́ → её, мы → нас, вы → вас, они́ → их. Ты меня́ слы́шишь? means Can you hear me? Я тебя́ ви́жу means I can see you. These forms often come before the verb; they can come after it too. The verb still agrees with the subject: я слы́шу, ты слы́шишь, она́ слы́шит.
pronoun-object.why: English changes I to me and he to him. Russian changes you too: ты becomes тебя́ when someone hears or sees you. The ending tells you the role even when the order changes: Ты меня́ слы́шишь? and Ты слы́шишь меня́? can both ask Can you hear me?

contrasts.says: English normally puts me after hear. Russian often puts меня́ before слы́шишь. Neither position is compulsory in Russian.
For the person heard or seen, use тебя́: Я тебя́ ви́жу. For the person receiving help, use тебе́: Я могу́ тебе́ помо́чь. Learn the form with the verb.
Use тебя́ with a friend you call ты. Use вас for someone you call вы, whether one person politely or several people.

mistakes.why: The person heard is the direct object: меня́, not the dative мне.
The person seen takes тебя́, not the dative тебе́.
Она́ is a subject form; the woman heard takes её.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

ni-ne.explain: Ничего́ and никогда́ work with the negative verb. Say Я ничего́ не хочу́ and Я никогда́ не пью ко́фе. The не stays even though English often uses a single word such as nothing or never. Nothing as an object here is ничего́. Не́чего belongs to a different construction; it cannot replace ничего́ in these sentences. A short reply can be just Ничего́: there is no verb to negate.
ni-ne.why: English can say I want nothing or I do not want anything. Russian uses ничего́ with не in the same clause. This does not turn the meaning positive. With never, keep both parts too: никогда́ не.

contrasts.says: Never already makes an English sentence negative. Russian still puts не before the verb: Я никогда́ не пью ко́фе.
Нет says there is none: У меня́ нет де́нег. A verb such as хочу́ instead uses не: Я ничего́ не хочу́.

mistakes.why: Никогда́ goes with не before the verb in this negative statement.
The object meaning not anything is ничего́ here, not не́чего.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

chto-clause.explain: Start with what someone thinks, knows or says, then use что to introduce the statement: Я ду́маю, что ма́ма уже́ до́ма. The statement can have its own subject: Я зна́ю, что ты рабо́таешь. Its verb agrees with that subject, not with the speaker of the first clause. Present-tense am, is and are are still left out: Я зна́ю, что ма́ма до́ма. A comma goes before что. In conversation, что can sometimes be omitted; these examples practice the version with it.
chto-clause.why: English often leaves out that: I think Mom is at home. Russian can make the link explicit with что. Time can set the scene before place, as in Я ду́маю, что встре́ча сего́дня в о́фисе, but Russian has no fixed rule that time must come first.

examples.text: Я думаю, что мама уже дома.
examples.means: I think Mom is already at home.
examples.literal: I think, that Mom already at home.

examples.text: Он говорит, что мама живёт в городе.
examples.means: He says Mom lives in the city.
examples.literal: He says, that Mom lives in city.

examples.text: Я думаю, что встреча сегодня в офисе.
examples.means: I think the meeting is in the office today.
examples.literal: I think, that meeting today in office.

examples.text: Я знаю, что ты сейчас гуляешь в парке.
examples.means: I know you're walking in the park now.
examples.literal: I know, that you now walk in park.

contrasts.says: Что ты чита́ешь? asks what you are reading. In Я ду́маю, что ма́ма уже́ до́ма, что introduces the statement being thought about.
Time and place can set the scene: Я ду́маю, что встре́ча сего́дня в о́фисе. Another order may put a different detail in focus; changing the order alone does not make a mistake.

mistakes.wrong: Я зна́ю, что ты сейча́с гуля́ю в па́рке.
mistakes.right: Я зна́ю, что ты сейча́с гуля́ешь в па́рке.
mistakes.why: The second subject is ты, so its verb is гуля́ешь. Я in the first clause does not control that verb.

mistakes.wrong: Он говори́т, что ма́ма живу́ в го́роде.
mistakes.right: Он говори́т, что ма́ма живёт в го́роде.
mistakes.why: Ма́ма is the subject inside the second clause, so use живёт.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

because.explain: Почему́ asks for a reason. Introduce the answer with потому́ что: Я опа́здываю, потому́ что не могу́ найти́ ключ. The phrase links a statement to its reason; it does not change the verb endings. Each clause can have its own subject. If the subject is unchanged and clear, it can be left out of the reason, as in this example. In this ordinary use, the comma comes before потому́ что, not between its two words.
because.why: English because corresponds to the two-word phrase потому́ что. Learn it together. The reason can describe an action, a location or a state: Я не могу́ помо́чь, потому́ что я за́нят. A woman says занята́.

examples.text: Я опаздываю, потому что не могу найти ключ.
examples.means: I'm running late because I can't find the key.
examples.literal: I run late, because not can find key.

examples.text: Мой друг опаздывает, потому что он у врача.
examples.means: My friend is running late because he's at the doctor's.
examples.literal: My friend runs late, because he at doctor's.

examples.text: Мама опаздывает, потому что не может найти телефон.
examples.means: Mom is running late because she can't find her phone.
examples.literal: Mom runs late, because not can find phone.

examples.text: Я хочу остаться дома, потому что здесь тихо.
examples.means: I want to stay at home because it is quiet here.
examples.literal: I want stay at home, because here quiet.

contrasts.says: Почему́ ты опа́здываешь? is the question. Я опа́здываю, потому́ что не могу́ найти́ ключ gives the reason.
Я ду́маю, что ма́ма уже́ до́ма reports a thought. Я опа́здываю, потому́ что не могу́ найти́ ключ gives a cause. Что alone and потому́ что do different jobs.

mistakes.wrong: Ты опа́здываешь, потому́ что ты рабо́таю в о́фисе?
mistakes.right: Ты опа́здываешь, потому́ что ты рабо́таешь в о́фисе?
mistakes.why: The reason has subject ты, so its verb is рабо́таешь. Потому́ что does not change the agreement.

mistakes.wrong: Я не могу́ помо́чь, потому́ что я за́няты.
mistakes.right: Я не могу́ помо́чь, потому́ что я за́нят.
mistakes.why: The reason still describes one speaker: за́нят for a man, занята́ for a woman, not the plural за́няты.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

verb-case.explain: Learn a verb together with the form of its object. For a person you are waiting for, ждать uses the accusative: Я жду тебя́, Мы ждём вас. For a person receiving help, помога́ть and помо́чь use the dative: Я помога́ю тебе́, Я могу́ помо́чь ма́ме. Neither needs a preposition for that person. This rule for ждать concerns people; it is not a claim that everything waited for always has the same case.
verb-case.why: English wait for needs for, while Russian ждёт can take the person directly. English help you has no to, while Russian still uses the dative тебе́. Translate the whole construction, not each English preposition separately.

contrasts.says: Тебя́ is the person heard or seen, and also the person waited for: Я тебя́ ви́жу; Я жду тебя́.
Тебе́ marks the person receiving help: Я помога́ю тебе́. The same case follows помо́чь: Я могу́ тебе́ помо́чь.

mistakes.why: The person waited for takes the object form тебя́, not the subject form ты.
Помога́ть takes the dative for the person helped: тебе́.
Помо́чь also takes the dative: ма́ме.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

genitive-plural.explain: A plural noun has different forms for different jobs. Год means year; after пять or ско́лько, use the genitive plural лет. Compare Ему́ три го́да with Ему́ пять лет. Age puts the person in the dative: ему́, сы́ну. A familiar example of the same case is У меня́ нет де́нег: де́ньги changes to де́нег after нет. Learn the genitive plural with each noun; the form cannot always be guessed from the ordinary plural. Quantities such as many and how many also use this case with countable things. The next lesson practices that pattern with books.
genitive-plural.why: English keeps years in both three years and five years. Russian distinguishes три го́да and пять лет. The case links the noun to the quantity. In an age expression, English makes the person the subject and adds is and old; Russian instead uses the dative person and the number of years.

examples.literal: How many years to your son?

examples.means: My son is already five years old.
examples.literal: To my son already five years.

contrasts.says: Де́ньги is the ordinary plural form. After нет, use the genitive plural де́нег.
Три го́да uses the genitive singular, but пять лет uses the genitive plural. Learn both forms with год.

mistakes.why: After пять, years has the genitive plural лет, not the singular form го́да.
Нет selects the genitive. The genitive plural of де́ньги is де́нег.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 61–80, open to correction.

numbers.explain: For these basic counts, one uses a singular noun and agrees with its gender: оди́н стол, одна́ кни́га. Two, three and four take the genitive singular; here practice два стола́, три стола́ and две кни́ги. Five takes the genitive plural: пять столо́в, пять книг. The form кни́ги here is genitive singular even though the same written form can also mean books elsewhere. Два is used with masculine and neuter nouns, две with feminine nouns. If the noun is understood, leave it out: У тебя́ одна́ кни́га, а у меня́ две. Larger numbers and counts after prepositions need further patterns; this lesson is about the basic counts shown here.
numbers.why: English normally puts a plural noun after any number larger than one. Russian makes a distinction between два стола́ and пять столо́в. It also remembers the gender of an omitted noun: две still refers to feminine кни́ги. With the noun left out, Russian says the number alone: У меня́ две.

examples.text: У тебя одна книга, а у меня две.
examples.means: You have one book, and I have two.
examples.literal: At you one book, and at me two.

contrasts.says: Пять книг uses the plural genitive. Две кни́ги uses the singular genitive even though two books are meant.
The choice of оди́н or одна́, and of два or две, follows the noun, not the person who owns it.

mistakes.why: After два, стол takes its genitive singular form стола́.
Пять needs the genitive plural, not the prepositional plural кни́гах.
Кни́га is feminine, so one is одна́.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 61–80, open to correction.

chtoby.explain: First say what someone does, then give the purpose with что́бы and an infinitive: Я иду́ в парк, что́бы безопа́сно гуля́ть. The person going is also the person walking, so no second subject is needed. The purpose can describe an activity, гуля́ть, or a bounded result, отдохну́ть. Что́бы does not automatically require one aspect. In Останови́сь здесь, что́бы позвони́ть ма́ме, both actions concern the person addressed. A comma separates the main action from its purpose. A different person in the purpose clause needs a construction taught in a later round.
chtoby.why: English often expresses purpose with to alone: go home to rest. Russian can say it with что́бы, which these lessons use; after a verb of going, a bare infinitive works too: Мы идём домо́й отдохну́ть. This differs from an infinitive directly after хочу́ or могу́, where no purpose connector is needed. It also differs from потому́ что, which explains a cause.

examples.text: Я иду в парк, чтобы безопасно гулять.
examples.means: I'm going to the park to walk safely.
examples.literal: I go to park, in order to safely walk.
Stop here, in order to call to Mom.
We go home, in order to rest.

contrasts.says: Потому́ что introduces the reason something happens. Что́бы introduces the intended purpose; that purpose need not already be achieved.
Я хочу́ отдохну́ть has an infinitive directly after хочу́. Мы идём домо́й, что́бы отдохну́ть adds the purpose of going home.

mistakes.why: For this same-person purpose, use an infinitive, not the present-tense form отдыха́ем.

mistakes.wrong: Я иду́ в парк, что́бы безопа́сно гуля́ю.
mistakes.right: Я иду́ в парк, что́бы безопа́сно гуля́ть.
mistakes.why: Гуля́ю is a finite present form. The purpose here needs the infinitive гуля́ть.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 61–80, open to correction.

pronoun-cases.explain: The six cases give a pronoun different jobs. Я is nominative, the subject. У меня́ uses genitive for the holder; ждёт меня́ uses accusative for the person awaited. Помога́ет мне uses dative for the recipient. Со мной uses instrumental for a companion; обо мне uses prepositional for a topic. The same spelling мне has two jobs: the surrounding words tell you which. For ты, compare ты, тебя́, тебе́, тобо́й. For мы, familiar нас becomes нам for a recipient and на́ми after с. For вы, use вас, вам or ва́ми as needed. Learn the form with the verb or preposition. The preposition обо is unstressed in обо мне; the stress falls on мне. Third-person forms after prepositions come later.
pronoun-cases.why: English keeps you in I see you, I help you and with you. Russian distinguishes тебя́, тебе́ and тобо́й. English me also covers both мне and меня́. These forms show the role even when the order changes; they are not interchangeable just because English uses the same word.

examples.text: Ты мне помогаешь, а я тебе.
examples.means: You help me, and I help you.
examples.literal: You to me help, and I to you.

examples.text: Это для тебя, а не для меня.
examples.means: This is for you, not for me.
examples.literal: This for you, and not for me.

examples.text: Мама ждёт меня, а не тебя.
examples.means: Mom is waiting for me, not you.
examples.literal: Mom waits for me, and not you.

examples.means: She wants to talk to me.

contrasts.says: Меня́ and тебя́ name a direct object in ждёт меня́ or ви́дит тебя́. The full set also includes мне and тебе́ for recipients and мной and тобо́й for companions.
Мне in помога́ет мне is dative. The identical мне in обо мне is prepositional: обо selects that case.
Use тебе́ and тобо́й with a friend. For polite or plural вы, familiar вам and ва́ми fill these roles: помо́чь вам, с ва́ми.

mistakes.why: Помога́ть takes the dative recipient мне, not the accusative меня́.
After обо for the topic, use prepositional мне.
After со for a companion, use instrumental мной, not subject я.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 81–100, open to correction.

reflexive.explain: The ending -ся or -сь is part of the verb, not a separate pronoun. Change the person before it: я бою́сь, ты бои́шься, он бои́тся. In these forms, -сь follows a vowel and -ся a consonant letter or the soft sign ь. The label reflexive does not mean every verb translates with yourself: боя́ться means be afraid, учи́ться means learn or study, and начина́ться means begin. Some verbs describe something done to oneself, some mutual contact, some a state or event. Learn each whole verb, its meaning and any case or preposition it needs; adding -ся freely does not guarantee a word with the intended meaning. Watch spelling in verbs like боя́ться: the infinitive has -ться, the third-person form -тся (он бои́тся). The phone-call lesson later practices mutual contact.
reflexive.why: English often uses a plain verb or be plus an adjective where Russian has a verb in -ся: Я бою́сь means I am afraid; Я учу́сь means I am learning. Do not add a separate yourself to every English translation. The whole Russian word carries the meaning.

examples.means: I’m afraid to watch this film.
examples.literal: I am afraid watch this film.

examples.means: My sister is afraid to watch too.

contrasts.says: The person still matters: я бою́сь, ты бои́шься. Keeping -ся or -сь does not replace the ordinary person endings.
Do not confuse the soft sign of an infinitive in -ться with a third-person form in -тся. Compare the dictionary verb боя́ться with он бои́тся.
The ending does not choose aspect: учи́ться describes learning, while познако́миться presents becoming acquainted as a whole event. Learn aspect with the verb too.

mistakes.why: For я, use бою́сь; бои́шься goes with ты. Keep the reflexive ending.
The third-person form бои́тся has no soft sign before -ся. This is a verb-form spelling error, not a different aspect.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 81–100, open to correction.

li.explain: After know, want to know or check, a question can become part of a larger sentence. If the question asks where, keep где: Ты зна́ешь, где мой телефо́н? If it asks for yes or no, use ли. Put the questioned word or group before ли: до́ма ли сестра́, рабо́тает ли А́нна, пра́вильно ли я записа́л и́мя. This lesson uses simple one-word focuses. Ли cannot introduce the clause from the front like English whether. Put a comma before the embedded question. The ending of the verb still agrees with its own subject. English if can also mean whether here; this is not a conditional sentence.
li.why: English puts whether or if before the whole embedded clause. Russian puts ли after the word or group it questions. Where is different: it asks for a location, so где stays. A statement with что says what is believed or known; a clause with ли leaves a yes/no question open.

examples.means: Do you know where my phone is?

examples.text: Я не знаю, дома ли сестра.
examples.means: I don’t know whether my sister is home.
examples.literal: I not know, at home whether sister.

examples.text: Ты знаешь, работает ли Анна сегодня?
examples.means: Do you know whether Anna is working today?
examples.literal: You know, works whether Anna today?

examples.text: Я не знаю, есть ли у тебя время.
examples.means: I don’t know whether you have time.
examples.literal: I not know, is whether at you time.

examples.text: Проверь, правильно ли я записал имя.
examples.means: Check whether I wrote the name down correctly.
examples.literal: Check, correctly whether I wrote down name.

contrasts.says: Где asks for a place, so it stays at the start of the embedded question. Ли marks a yes/no question and follows its focus.
Я зна́ю, что сестра́ до́ма states that she is home. Я не зна́ю, до́ма ли сестра́ leaves that question open.

mistakes.wrong: Я не зна́ю, ли до́ма сестра́.
mistakes.right: Я не зна́ю, до́ма ли сестра́.
mistakes.why: Ли follows the questioned до́ма; it does not begin the clause.

mistakes.wrong: Прове́рь, ли пра́вильно я записа́л и́мя.
mistakes.right: Прове́рь, пра́вильно ли я записа́л и́мя.
mistakes.why: Put ли after пра́вильно, the point being checked.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 81–100, open to correction.

conditional.explain: Бы with a past-form verb expresses a wish, an imagined possibility or a softened request. Вы могли́ бы мне помо́чь? asks for help now, not about past ability. The verb still agrees: a man says Я хоте́л бы помо́чь, a woman Я хоте́ла бы помо́чь; with мы or вы, use хоте́ли бы or могли́ бы. Write бы separately. It can follow the verb or come earlier: Я хоте́л бы спроси́ть and Я бы хоте́л спроси́ть are both natural. After хоте́л бы or мог бы, another action takes the infinitive. Keep ты with a friend and вы with an unfamiliar adult. Adding бы does not make ты a formal form of address.
conditional.why: English uses would like or could for these wishes and requests. Russian combines a past-form verb with бы, so its gender or plural ending remains visible even when the wish concerns now or tomorrow. Вы не могли́ бы повтори́ть? is a conventional polite request; the negative wording does not mean the speaker wants no repetition.

examples.literal: You could would to me help?
I wanted would help to you.

examples.text: Я хотела бы поговорить с вами.
examples.means: I'd like to talk to you.
examples.literal: I wanted would talk with you.

examples.text: Я бы хотел спросить о работе.
examples.means: I'd like to ask about work.
examples.literal: I would wanted ask about work.

contrasts.says: The past form supplies the agreement, but бы changes the meaning: Я хоте́л бы помо́чь is a present wish, not a statement that the speaker wanted to help earlier.
Only the first verb has the past-form ending: Я хоте́л бы помо́чь. The second action is an infinitive.
Вы могли́ бы помо́чь? addresses an unfamiliar adult politely. Ты мог бы помо́чь? addresses a male friend; to a female friend, Ты могла́ бы помо́чь?

mistakes.why: Бы does not remove agreement. With мы, use plural могли́, not singular мог.
After хоте́л бы, use an infinitive for the intended action. Помога́ю is a finite present form.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 101–120, open to correction.

impersonal.explain: Some sentences have no nominative subject. In Мне удо́бно учи́ться до́ма, мне names the person for whom studying at home works well. Use dative мне, тебе́, нам or вам, and keep удо́бно unchanged. Ну́жно with an infinitive expresses a need: Мне ну́жно учи́ться. Тру́дно describes difficulty in the same way. The person can be left understood: Мо́жно учи́ться вме́сте expresses permission or possibility. Do not insert a Russian word for it just because English says it is convenient or it is possible. Learn the describing word and the construction together.
impersonal.why: English often makes I or you the subject: I need to study, or I find studying difficult. Russian can instead name the person in the dative and describe the need or experience without a subject. This pattern does not make every noun after мне an object: in Мне нужна́ кни́га, кни́га is the subject and нужна́ agrees with it.

examples.means: Studying at home works well for me.
examples.literal: To me convenient study at home.

examples.means: Is it comfortable for you to read on your phone?
examples.literal: To you comfortable read on phone?

examples.means: Studying in the evening suits me.
examples.literal: To me convenient study in the evening.

examples.means: We can study together after work.

contrasts.says: Ну́жно with an infinitive stays unchanged: Мне ну́жно учи́ться. With a noun as subject, the short adjective agrees: Мне нужна́ кни́га; Мне ну́жен телефо́н.
Мне and тебе́ name the person experiencing the need or difficulty. They are not subject forms я and ты.
The activity after удо́бно or мо́жно is an infinitive: Мне удо́бно чита́ть; Мо́жно учи́ться вме́сте.

mistakes.why: For the person experiencing this convenience, use dative мне. Я is a subject form and does not fit this construction.
After ну́жно, use the infinitive учи́ться, not the finite present учу́сь.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 101–120, open to correction.

motion-both-ways.explain: Ходи́ть and е́здить are imperfective verbs. Use them for repeated trips: Я ча́сто хожу́ в э́тот парк. Use ходи́ть for going on foot and е́здить for transport. In the past, ходи́л or е́здил can report a visit there and back: Вчера́ я ходи́л в э́тот парк. The past can also describe a repeated habit; the surrounding words decide. Идти́ and е́хать instead focus on movement in one direction, such as a trip in progress. These are not aspect pairs: neither member becomes perfective just because it concerns one trip. Learn the forms: я хожу́, вы хо́дите; я е́зжу, вы е́здите. A woman says ходи́ла or е́здила about a past visit.
motion-both-ways.why: English go and went cover both kinds of movement. Russian asks how you view the trip. Frequency words help in these examples, but they do not mechanically choose the verb: a repeated trip can also be described from the point of view of its one-way journey. Do not mark every sentence with идти́ and ча́сто as wrong. Here the regular-trip and return-visit meanings are taught in clear contexts.

examples.text: Вы часто ходите в этот парк?
examples.means: Do you often walk to this park?
examples.literal: You often go on foot to this park?

examples.text: Вчера я ходил в этот парк.
examples.means: I went to this park yesterday.
examples.literal: Yesterday I went to this park and came back.

examples.text: Вы часто ездите в этот город?
examples.means: Do you often travel to this city?
examples.literal: You often go by transport to this city?

examples.text: Вы сейчас едете прямо в город?
examples.means: Are you traveling straight to the city now?
examples.literal: You now are going straight to city?

contrasts.says: Идти́ and е́хать focus on movement in one direction. Ходи́ть and е́здить can cover regular trips or past visits there and back.
Ходи́ть and е́здить are imperfective, as are идти́ and е́хать. Пое́хал presents setting off; е́здил can report a visit. These different meanings are not a correct/wrong pair.
Past agreement remains: a man says я ходи́л, a woman я ходи́ла. Present forms instead follow person: я хожу́, вы хо́дите.

mistakes.wrong: Я ча́сто хо́дите в э́тот парк.
mistakes.right: Я ча́сто хожу́ в э́тот парк.
mistakes.why: Ходи́ть still agrees with its subject: я takes хожу́. Хо́дите is the present form for вы.

mistakes.wrong: Вы ча́сто е́зжу в э́тот го́род?
mistakes.right: Вы ча́сто е́здите в э́тот го́род?
mistakes.why: Use е́здите with вы, not the first-person е́зжу.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 121–140, open to correction.

if-when.explain: Е́сли gives a condition that may or may not be met. Когда́ gives the time of an expected event. In these future situations, use future forms in both parts: Е́сли ты бу́дешь до́ма, я приду́. Russian does not replace the future with a present just because the clause begins with е́сли or когда́. The clause can come first: Когда́ я приду́ домо́й, я позвоню́ тебе́. It can also come last: Я позвоню́ тебе́, когда́ приду́ домо́й. A clear repeated subject may be left understood. Write a comma between the clauses. A request can be the main clause too: Когда́ ты бу́дешь до́ма, позвони́ мне.
if-when.why: English normally says when I get home, even about tomorrow. Russian says когда́ я приду́ домо́й. Future comes from the event being future, not from a blanket rule for the conjunction: present forms can describe present conditions or habits, and past forms can describe past events. Е́сли means conditional if here; an embedded yes/no question uses the earlier ли construction.

examples.text: Когда я приду домой, я позвоню тебе.
examples.means: When I get home, I'll call you.
examples.literal: When I will come home, I will call to you.

examples.text: Я позвоню тебе, когда приду домой.
examples.means: I'll call you when I get home.
examples.literal: I will call to you, when will come home.

examples.text: Если ты будешь дома, я приду.
examples.means: If you're at home, I'll come over.
examples.literal: If you will be at home, I will come.

examples.text: Когда ты будешь дома, позвони мне.
examples.means: When you're at home, call me.
examples.literal: When you will be at home, call to me.

contrasts.says: The ordinary future constructions still apply: бу́дешь до́ма, бу́дем пить чай, приду́. Do not combine бу́ду with a perfective infinitive such as прийти́.
Е́сли introduces a condition; ли marks an embedded yes/no question. English if can translate either, but the Russian constructions differ.
Когда́ can ask when on its own or join a time clause to another clause. In Когда́ я приду́ домо́й, я позвоню́ тебе́, it gives a time rather than asking a question.

mistakes.wrong: Е́сли ты бу́ду до́ма, я приду́.
mistakes.right: Е́сли ты бу́дешь до́ма, я приду́.
mistakes.why: The verb inside the condition agrees with its own subject ты: бу́дешь.

mistakes.wrong: Я позвоню́ тебе́, когда́ бу́ду прийти́ домо́й.
mistakes.right: Я позвоню́ тебе́, когда́ приду́ домо́й.
mistakes.why: Прийти́ is perfective. Its future is приду́, without бу́ду and an infinitive.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 121–140, open to correction.

relative.explain: A relative clause identifies or describes a noun: Э́то текст, кото́рый я не понима́ю. Кото́рый gets its gender and number from the noun it refers back to. Its case comes from the role it plays inside its own clause. In Э́то кни́га, кото́рую я хочу́ прочита́ть, кни́га is the noun being identified, but кото́рую is the feminine accusative object of прочита́ть. Compare masculine текст, кото́рый and neuter сло́во, кото́рое when these inanimate words are objects. Keep кото́рый even when English can omit that or which. Put a comma before the clause; if the main sentence continues afterwards, close the relative clause with another comma.
relative.why: English can say the book you are reading. Russian needs the link: кни́га, кото́рую ты чита́ешь. The ending carries information that English which does not show. Do not simply copy the case of the earlier noun: each clause assigns its own roles. Later examples extend the same rule to people as objects.

examples.text: Это текст, который я не понимаю.
examples.means: This is a text I don't understand.
examples.literal: This text, which I not understand.

examples.text: Это книга, которую я хочу прочитать.
examples.means: This is a book I want to read.
examples.literal: This book, which I want read through.

examples.text: Книга, которую ты читаешь, очень интересная.
examples.means: The book you're reading is very interesting.
examples.literal: Book, which you read, very interesting.

examples.text: Повтори слово, которое ты не понимаешь.
examples.means: Repeat the word you don't understand.
examples.literal: Repeat word, which you not understand.

contrasts.says: Кото́рый follows the noun in gender and number, like an adjective. Its case, however, belongs to its role inside the relative clause.
In кни́га, кото́рую я чита́ю, кото́рую is the object of чита́ю. The earlier кни́га does not force it to be nominative.
Что introduces the content of a statement after a verb such as знать. Кото́рый here refers back to a noun and describes which thing is meant.

mistakes.wrong: Э́то текст, кото́рую я не понима́ю.
mistakes.right: Э́то текст, кото́рый я не понима́ю.
mistakes.why: Текст is masculine, so feminine кото́рую cannot refer to it.

mistakes.wrong: Кни́га, кото́рый ты чита́ешь, о́чень интере́сная.
mistakes.right: Кни́га, кото́рую ты чита́ешь, о́чень интере́сная.
mistakes.why: Кни́га is feminine and is being read inside the relative clause: кото́рую, a feminine accusative form.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 121–140, open to correction.

motion-prefix.explain: A prefix changes what part of a journey the verb presents. Here в- gives entry in войти́, вы- exit in вы́йти, при- arrival in прийти́, у- departure in уйти́, and за- a brief visit in зайти́. These whole verbs are perfective. Я вошёл в ко́мнату reports entry as a completed event; Я вы́йду, когда́ ты придёшь gives future events. Do not add бу́ду to a perfective infinitive. Keep the familiar case patterns: в ко́мнату for the destination, к тебе́ for a visit to your place, ко мне before мне. Learn each verb as a word: a prefix is not a guarantee that every invented combination exists. The road lesson later extends the pattern to crossing.
motion-prefix.why: English often uses a separate word such as in, out, or away. Russian can put this part of the meaning in a prefix. Prefixes and aspect are related but not identical: these particular verbs are perfective, while related verbs can describe an ongoing or repeated journey. The regular-trip distinction from ходи́ть and е́здить still matters. This lesson does not present an arbitrary prefix as a universal perfective switch.

examples.text: Мы смогли открыть дверь и войти.
examples.means: We managed to get the door open and go in.
examples.literal: We managed open door and enter.

examples.means: I'll come outside when you arrive.
examples.literal: I will go out, when you will arrive.

examples.text: Я хочу зайти к тебе после работы.
examples.means: I want to stop by your place after work.
examples.literal: I want stop by to you after work.

contrasts.says: The verbs войти́ and вы́йти present a bounded event. Their future forms do not take бу́ду plus an infinitive.
Ходи́ть and е́здить can describe regular trips or past visits there and back. The prefixed verbs here instead specify entry, exit, arrival, departure, or a brief visit.
The prefix does not remove the preposition or its case: войти́ в ко́мнату, зайти́ к тебе́.

mistakes.wrong: Я бу́ду вы́йти, когда́ ты придёшь.
mistakes.why: Вы́йти is perfective. Use its own future form вы́йду.

mistakes.wrong: Я хочу́ зайти́ к тебя́ по́сле рабо́ты.
mistakes.right: Я хочу́ зайти́ к тебе́ по́сле рабо́ты.
mistakes.why: К takes the dative тебе́, not accusative or genitive тебя́.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 141–160, open to correction.

passive.explain: Russian can focus on what receives an action. Short passive forms agree with the thing affected: Э́тот стол сде́лан для ма́мы; Рабо́та уже́ сде́лана; Всё уже́ сде́лано. Present is is left out. For a past state, use an agreeing past form of быть: Дверь была́ закры́та, когда́ я пришёл. A woman describing her arrival says пришла́; была́ закры́та still follows дверь. These examples leave out who did the work; it can be named, but often isn't the point. A verb in -ся can instead describe a process: Ря́дом стро́ится но́вый дом. Стро́ится agrees with the singular дом or шко́ла. This is one use of -ся, not the meaning of every verb with that ending.
passive.why: English often uses be plus a participle for both a state and an action in progress. Russian distinguishes the agreeing result form from the process expressed by стро́ится. A result such as дверь закры́та can simply describe the present state; it does not need to recount the act of closing. Ordinary conversation also uses active verbs when the doer matters.

examples.means: This table was made for Mom.
A new house is being built nearby.
examples.literal: Nearby is being built new house.

contrasts.says: Like familiar ready or busy forms, сде́лан, сде́лана and сде́лано agree with the subject. These forms specifically describe the result of an action.
Стро́ится is passive here. Бои́тся and обща́юсь have other meanings; the ending alone cannot tell you the construction.
Дверь была́ закры́та describes a past state. Был, была́ or бы́ло follows the subject, not the speaker.

mistakes.why: Рабо́та is feminine, so its result form is сде́лана.
Всё takes a neuter result form: сде́лано.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 141–160, open to correction.

superlative.explain: To identify the biggest, most convenient, or most comfortable option in a group, use са́мый with the ordinary adjective. Compare са́мый большо́й дом, са́мая больша́я ко́мната, and са́мое удо́бное ме́сто. Са́мый and the adjective both match the noun. When the room is the object of посмотре́ть, use са́мую большу́ю ко́мнату. A phrase such as в дере́вне names the group being considered; the group may also be clear from the conversation. Russian adds no separate word for the English the. The comparison lesson later introduces the distinct forms for better and more.
superlative.why: English can put an ending on biggest or use most convenient. This Russian construction keeps the ordinary adjective and adds a separate agreeing word. Gender and case therefore appear on two words. This is the greatest degree in the relevant group; it need not be the greatest everywhere.

examples.text: Это самый большой дом в деревне.
examples.means: This is the biggest house in the village.
examples.literal: This most big house in village.

examples.text: Это самая большая комната в доме.
examples.means: This is the biggest room in the house.
examples.literal: This most big room in house.

examples.text: Я хочу посмотреть самую большую комнату.
examples.means: I want to see the biggest room.
examples.literal: I want see most big room.

examples.text: Это самое удобное место для стола.
examples.means: This is the most convenient spot for the table.
examples.literal: This most convenient place for table.

contrasts.says: Са́мый has agreeing forms too: са́мая больша́я ко́мната. Do not leave са́мый unchanged when the noun changes.
A feminine object requires both са́мую and большу́ю: посмотре́ть са́мую большу́ю ко́мнату.

mistakes.wrong: Э́то са́мый больша́я ко́мната в до́ме.
mistakes.right: Э́то са́мая больша́я ко́мната в до́ме.
mistakes.why: Ко́мната is feminine. Use са́мая with больша́я.

mistakes.wrong: Я хочу́ посмотре́ть са́мая большу́ю ко́мнату.
mistakes.right: Я хочу́ посмотре́ть са́мую большу́ю ко́мнату.
mistakes.why: The object is accusative. Both са́мую and большу́ю take that case.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 141–160, open to correction.

comparative.explain: Use лу́чше for better, ху́же for worse, and бо́льше for more. The forms themselves do not change to match a person: Ты чита́ешь лу́чше, чем я. Чем introduces what you compare with; a comma comes before it in these examples. For an amount, keep the following noun in the genitive: бо́льше вре́мени, бо́льше ме́ста. The reference point can stay understood. With an action, лу́чше can recommend an alternative or express a choice: Дава́й лу́чше оста́немся до́ма; Я лу́чше позвоню́, чем бу́ду ждать. This preference use is related in meaning but is not an extra degree ending. Learn these frequent forms first; other comparisons have other forms.
comparative.why: English uses better and worse irregularly too. Russian also uses these words in impersonal statements: Сего́дня мне ху́же, чем вчера́. The dative мне identifies who feels worse. A recommendation with лу́чше often becomes instead or would rather in natural English. Do not mechanically translate it as better in every sentence.

examples.means: You read better than I do.
I feel worse today than yesterday.
examples.literal: Today to me worse, than yesterday.

examples.text: Я лучше позвоню, чем буду ждать.
examples.literal: I better will call, than will wait.

contrasts.says: Бо́льше governs the quantity: бо́льше вре́мени, бо́льше ме́ста. The endings remain important even when English simply says more time or more space.
Са́мый большо́й identifies the biggest within a group. Бо́льше expresses a greater amount or size relative to something, often understood.
Мне ху́же describes how I feel, with dative мне and unchanged ху́же.

mistakes.why: The quantity after бо́льше is genitive: вре́мени.
Ме́сто becomes genitive ме́ста after бо́льше.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 141–160, open to correction.

n-forms.explain: Third-person personal pronouns change after the prepositions shown here. For он, compare у него́, к нему́, с ним, о нём. For она́, use у неё and с ней or о ней. For они́, use с ни́ми and о них. The initial н is only part of the choice: the preposition still governs the case. A thing follows its grammatical gender: фильм is masculine, so о нём can mean about it; исто́рия is feminine, so о ней can mean about it. Distinguish possession: с его́ бра́том means with his brother. Here с governs бра́том, and possessive его́ does not change. Learn other prepositions with their pronoun forms; this is not a rule to put н after every possible preposition.
n-forms.why: English it stays it after about. Russian remembers both the noun’s gender and the pronoun’s case. English his and him are different words, but Russian его́ can be a possessive or a personal form. Ask whether the pronoun itself follows the preposition or instead describes the owner of a following noun.

examples.text: Это новый фильм. Что ты о нём думаешь?
examples.means: This is a new film. What do you think of it?
examples.literal: This new film. What you about it think?

examples.means: I want to talk to him.

examples.text: У неё есть книга об этом фильме.
examples.means: She has a book about this film.
examples.literal: At her exists book about this film.

examples.text: Я хочу посмотреть фильм с ними.
examples.means: I want to watch the film with them.
examples.literal: I want watch film with them.

contrasts.says: Compare с ним, with him, and с его́ бра́том, with his brother. Possessive его́, её and их stay unchanged.
К нему́ needs the dative, с ним the instrumental, and о нём the prepositional. Adding н does not make the cases interchangeable.
О нём can refer to фильм; о ней can refer to исто́рия. English translates both as about it.

mistakes.why: С meaning with takes instrumental ним here.

mistakes.wrong: Я зайду́ к него́ по́сле рабо́ты.
mistakes.right: Я зайду́ к нему́ по́сле рабо́ты.
mistakes.why: К takes dative нему́. Genitive него́ is used after у in these lessons.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 141–160, open to correction.

time.explain: A time on the clock and the time of an event have different forms: Сейча́с полови́на тре́тьего says it is 2:30; Я приду́ в полови́не тре́тьего says when you will arrive. Russian counts half of the hour that is being completed, so тре́тьего points to the third hour, not to 3:30. At a whole hour, use в with the number: в два часа́. Два takes genitive singular часа́. For a weekday, в takes the accusative: в пя́тницу. For a calendar date answering when, use a genitive ordinal and a genitive month without a preposition: пе́рвого ма́я. These lessons teach those forms as useful models; learn other hours, weekdays and dates with their forms.
time.why: English at half past two counts from the hour already reached. Russian полови́на тре́тьего looks toward the third hour. English on appears with both Friday and May first; Russian distinguishes в пя́тницу from пе́рвого ма́я. A single English preposition therefore does not predict the Russian case.

examples.means: I'll come at half past two.
examples.literal: I will come at half of the third.

examples.text: В пятницу встреча в два часа.
examples.means: The meeting is at two o'clock on Friday.
examples.literal: On Friday meeting at two hours.

examples.means: I'll be at home on May first.
examples.literal: On the first of May I will be at home.

contrasts.says: В два часа́ keeps the counting form часа́ after два. The phrase gives an event time, not a duration.
Полови́на changes to полови́не after в for an event at half past the hour. The following тре́тьего stays genitive.
Пе́рвого ма́я uses genitive forms for both the day number and the month. В пя́тницу instead uses the accusative after в.

mistakes.why: For the time of the arrival, use в полови́не, with the prepositional ending.

mistakes.wrong: В пя́тницу встре́ча в две часа́.
mistakes.right: В пя́тницу встре́ча в два часа́.
mistakes.why: Час is masculine, so use два, not feminine две.
The month must be genitive ма́я in this calendar date.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 181–200, open to correction.

diminutive.explain: До́мик is a diminutive of дом. In the yard, it can name a small house for children to play in. It can also name an ordinary small house. Ма́мочка is an affectionate form of ма́ма: a child can say Ма́мочка, мо́жно поигра́ть во дворе́? It expresses closeness, not the size of the mother. The two words use different suffixes. Learn each established word instead of attaching an ending freely. The new noun keeps its ordinary grammar: э́тот до́мик, в до́мике, для дете́й. Affectionate forms suit close relationships and can sound out of place with a stranger.
diminutive.why: English may use little with a noun or a familiar name such as Mommy. Russian often builds that meaning into the word. Context decides whether smallness, affection, or both are intended. Not every word ending in these letters is a diminutive, and a familiar form does not automatically express affection in every tone.

examples.means: This little house is for children.
A child is sitting in the playhouse.
Mommy, can I play in the yard for a while?
examples.literal: Mommy, possible play a while in yard?
Mommy, look at my little house.

contrasts.says: До́мик is masculine like дом; ма́мочка is feminine like ма́ма. An agreeing word still follows the noun: э́тот до́мик.
The suffix does not freeze the word: до́мик becomes в до́мике for a location.
Ма́мочка is a close, affectionate family address. It does not replace polite вы when speaking to an unfamiliar adult.

mistakes.why: До́мик is masculine. Its demonstrative is э́тот, even when the house is small.
For a location after в, use prepositional до́мике, not instrumental до́миком.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 181–200, open to correction.

plural.explain: To talk about more than one thing, use a plural noun: the basic, or nominative, plural often ends in -ы or -и, and sometimes -а or -я, as in вопро́сы, ключи́ and слова́. Adjectives and words such as my or this match it: но́вые очки́, мои́ пла́ны, э́ти слова́. Some Russian words are normally plural even where English is not, such as де́ньги (money) and выходны́е (the weekend). Other jobs in the sentence can change these endings again.
plural.why: English leaves my and new unchanged before plural nouns, while Russian uses forms such as [[мои́]] and но́вые to match them.

examples.means: My plans for tomorrow are changing.

examples.text: Я хотел бы купить новые очки.
examples.means: I'd like to buy new glasses.
examples.literal: I wanted would buy new glasses

contrasts.says: In these basic plural forms, adjectives and possessives no longer distinguish masculine, feminine and neuter.
The ordinary plural кни́ги changes to книг after нет, so learning a plural also means learning its forms for other jobs.

mistakes.why: Вопро́сы is plural, so your must be plural ва́ши too.

mistakes.wrong: Я хоте́л бы купи́ть но́вый очки́.
mistakes.right: Я хоте́л бы купи́ть но́вые очки́.
mistakes.why: Очки́ is plural even for one pair of glasses, so use но́вые.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

adjective.explain: An adjective describes a noun and changes to match its gender, number and case: но́вый телефо́н, но́вая маши́на, но́вое ме́сто, но́вые очки́. Case means the noun's job in the sentence, and the adjective follows it: с но́вым телефо́ном, в но́вой маши́не. The endings on the adjective and noun need not look alike; they still show the same gender, number and case.
adjective.why: English keeps new the same in every phrase, but Russian uses [[но́вая]] with a feminine noun and changes the adjective again when its job changes.

examples.text: Ты можешь помочь с новым телефоном?
examples.means: Can you help with the new phone?
examples.literal: You can help with new phone

examples.text: Я хотел бы купить новые очки.
examples.means: I'd like to buy new glasses.
examples.literal: I wanted would buy new glasses

contrasts.says: The noun supplies the gender, and the adjective matches it even when the noun names a thing.
Мой and твой also match their noun, but possessive его́, её and их stay unchanged.

mistakes.why: Маши́на is feminine, so the adjective is но́вая.

mistakes.wrong: Ты мо́жешь помо́чь с но́вый телефо́ном?
mistakes.right: Ты мо́жешь помо́чь с но́вым телефо́ном?
mistakes.why: After с meaning with, both но́вым and телефо́ном take the instrumental.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

genitive.explain: The genitive often means of: маши́на ма́мы is Mom's car, and ча́шка ча́я is a cup of tea. It also follows words such as для (for), без (without), из (from inside) and у (at or by): для ма́мы, без са́хара, у меня́. Many amounts and numbers need it too, as in немно́го воды́ and де́сять мину́т. Learn the form with the word, since singular and plural nouns have different genitive endings.
genitive.why: English uses of, an apostrophe or a preposition without changing the noun, while Russian also marks the relationship in forms such as [[ма́мы]].

examples.means: I'd like a cup of tea.

examples.text: Я обычно пью кофе без сахара.
examples.means: I usually drink coffee without sugar.
examples.literal: I usually drink coffee without sugar

contrasts.says: Для ма́мы and dative ма́ме can both involve a recipient, but the preposition для requires the genitive.
Нет also takes the genitive to name what is absent: нет молока́.

mistakes.why: Для requires the genitive ма́мы.
The tea is what the cup contains, so of tea is genitive ча́я.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

genitive-negation.explain: Use нет to say that something is not there, and put the missing thing in the genitive: нет рабо́ты, нет молока́. With у меня́, this says I don't have it: У меня́ нет вре́мени. Plural things take the genitive plural too: нет книг. For future absence, use не бу́дет with the same case: не бу́дет вре́мени means there won't be time.
genitive-negation.why: English uses there isn't or don't have without changing the thing's name, but Russian puts it in the genitive after [[нет]].

examples.text: У меня нет книг о городе.
examples.means: I don't have any books about the city.
examples.literal: At me no books about city

examples.means: There's no room for the bag here.

contrasts.says: У меня́ есть рабо́та uses the basic subject form, while У меня́ нет рабо́ты uses the genitive.
Нет says something is absent, while не can deny an action or description, as in Я не чита́ю.

mistakes.why: After нет, рабо́та becomes genitive рабо́ты.
Вре́мя has the genitive form вре́мени after нет.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

dative.explain: The dative names someone receiving something or receiving help: дать тебе́ (give to you), помо́чь дру́гу (help a friend). It also names the person who feels, needs or likes something: Мне хо́лодно means I am cold, and Мне нужна́ по́мощь means I need help. With нра́вится, the thing liked is the subject and the person liking it is dative: Мне нра́вится фильм is like saying the film is pleasing to me.
dative.why: English makes I the subject of I like or I need, while Russian can use [[мне]], meaning to me, for that person.

examples.literal: I can help to a friend

examples.means: I want to give you a number.
examples.literal: I want give to you number
To me very is pleasing this film

contrasts.says: Russian verbs choose their cases: ви́жу дру́га uses an accusative object, but помога́ю дру́гу needs the dative.
У меня́ means at me and uses the genitive, while мне is dative with no у.

mistakes.why: Помо́чь takes the dative person дру́гу.
The film is the subject of нра́вится, so the person liking it is dative мне.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

instrumental.explain: After с meaning with, use the instrumental: с дру́гом, с ма́мой, с молоко́м. Before мной, use со: со мной means with me. The same case says what someone works as, without с: рабо́тает врачо́м means works as a doctor. After за, it can name what you are going to get: иду́ за водо́й means I am going to get water.
instrumental.why: English keeps milk unchanged after with, while Russian changes молоко́ to [[молоко́м]] after с.

examples.means: I'm going home with a friend.
My sister works as a doctor.
examples.literal: My sister works as a doctor

contrasts.says: Compare с молоко́м (with milk) and без молока́ (without milk): each preposition requires its own case.
За водо́й after a verb of going means to get water, while за во́ду after paying means for the water.

mistakes.why: С meaning with requires instrumental соба́кой.
After рабо́тает, the profession takes the instrumental врачо́м.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

past.explain: In the past, a singular verb matches the subject's gender instead of changing for I, you or he: он был, она́ была́, оно́ бы́ло. Many past forms end in -л for masculine, -ла for feminine and -ло for neuter; the plural uses -ли, as in они́ бы́ли. A man says я купи́л and a woman says я купи́ла, so the speaker matters when the subject is I. Some past forms describe a result still felt now: Я уста́л means I am tired.
past.why: English made does not show gender, while Russian [[де́лала]] identifies a feminine singular subject.

examples.means: I'm tired and want to rest.
examples.literal: I got tired and want rest

contrasts.says: Present endings distinguish я чита́ю and ты чита́ешь, but past чита́л fits either pronoun when its subject is a man.
Чита́л and прочита́л are both masculine past forms; the aspect choice says whether the reading is presented as a completed whole.

mistakes.why: Ма́ма is the feminine subject, so the past form is де́лала.
With plural мы, use бы́ли regardless of the speakers' genders.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

future.explain: Use бу́ду, бу́дешь or another future form of быть with an imperfective infinitive for an action viewed as ongoing, repeated or without focusing on completion: бу́ду чита́ть. A perfective verb presents a whole action in its own future form, such as прочита́ю, without бу́ду. Russian can also use a present form for a plan, as in За́втра я рабо́таю, and бу́дет for what there will be, as in За́втра бу́дет дождь. After е́сли (if) or когда́ (when), a future event keeps its future form: е́сли ты бу́дешь до́ма.
future.why: English often uses will with either kind of action, but Russian [[прочита́ю]] already carries the future meaning without a separate will.

examples.means: Tomorrow I'll be working at home.
examples.literal: Tomorrow I will work at home

examples.means: Tomorrow I'll finish reading this book.
examples.literal: Tomorrow I will read through this book

examples.text: Я помню, что ты работаешь завтра.
examples.means: I remember that you're working tomorrow.
examples.literal: I remember, that you work tomorrow

examples.text: Если ты будешь дома, я приду.
examples.means: If you're at home, I'll come over.
examples.literal: If you will be at home, I will come

contrasts.says: Бу́ду чита́ть focuses on the reading, while прочита́ю presents reading it through as a whole.
English says if you are home for a future condition, where Russian can say е́сли ты бу́дешь до́ма.

mistakes.why: The future helper agrees with я, so use бу́ду and leave рабо́тать in its infinitive form.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

aspect.explain: Many Russian verbs come in pairs that show how you view an action. The imperfective, such as чита́ть, describes it going on, happening repeatedly or simply having happened, without focusing on completion. The perfective, such as прочита́ть, presents it as a whole, with its endpoint in view. Я чита́л does not by itself say whether I finished, while Я прочита́л says I read it through.
aspect.why: English can add words such as was reading or read through, while Russian chooses a different verb, such as [[прочита́л]], to show the completed whole.

examples.means: I've already finished reading this book.
examples.literal: I already read through this book

examples.means: Have you finished reading this book yet?
examples.literal: You already read through this book

contrasts.says: Both чита́л and прочита́л are past tense, so choosing a completed whole is a separate choice from placing the action in the past.
The future is бу́ду чита́ть for the imperfective and прочита́ю for the perfective, never бу́ду прочита́ть.

mistakes.wrong: За́втра я бу́ду прочита́ть э́ту кни́гу.
mistakes.why: Perfective прочита́ть makes its own future, прочита́ю; only an imperfective infinitive such as чита́ть goes with бу́ду.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

motion.explain: For a person making one trip now or planned, идти́ is going on foot and е́хать is going by vehicle. The same words can mean come or leave when the situation calls for it. Ходи́ть and е́здить describe regular trips or, in the past, a visit there and back; пойти́ and пое́хать present setting off on one trip. Learn the changing forms with each verb: я иду́, мы идём; я е́ду, мы е́дем.
motion.why: English go can cover walking and riding, while Russian [[иду́]] and е́ду distinguish them when a person is making a trip.

examples.text: Обычно езжу на поезде, а сегодня еду на машине.
examples.means: I usually travel by train, but today I am going by car.
examples.literal: Usually travel on train, but today am going on car

examples.means: I went to the park on foot.

examples.literal: I will go by train tomorrow

contrasts.says: Идти́ and ходи́ть are both imperfective, as are е́хать and е́здить, so the one-way or regular-trip choice is separate from aspect.
The motion verb describes the journey, while домо́й names its destination and до́ма means at home.

mistakes.why: Идти́ changes for the person: я иду́, but он идёт.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

new-last.explain: Russian often starts with the setting or what is already known and puts the new information near the end. That lets a subject follow its verb: На столе́ лежи́т ключ introduces the key after saying where it is. This is a common way to organize information, not a fixed order; context and the word you emphasize can change the order.
new-last.why: English often introduces a new thing with there is, while Russian can put [[ключ]] after the verb to introduce the key.

examples.means: There's a key on the table.
My family is in the photo.
My mom used to live here.

contrasts.says: Coming after a verb does not make a word its object: кни́га is still the subject in Внутри́ лежи́т кни́га.
A place can come first even without a present-tense is: На фотогра́фии моя́ семья́.

mistakes.why: Кни́га is what is lying there, so it stays in the subject form even after the verb.
The verb still matches feminine ма́ма even when the subject comes later.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

imperative.explain: To ask or tell someone to do something, use a command form, usually without a subject: Иди́ домо́й, Откро́й дверь, Дай мне знать. For several people or a polite request to one person, add -те to the singular command: иди́те, откро́йте, да́йте. Learn the command with the verb, since the forms differ. Пожа́луйста means please and can make the request gentler, but it does not change the verb form.
imperative.why: English uses the same open for one listener or several, while Russian [[откро́йте]] marks plural or polite address.

examples.means: Have a look at this room, please.
examples.literal: Have a look at this room, please

contrasts.says: Use иди́ for someone you address as ты, and иди́те for someone you address as вы.
